title: Σαρπηδὼν καὶ Πάτροκλος
about: Patroclus drives the Trojans back from the city toward the ships and takes requital in the space between the ships, the river and the wall: he kills Pronous, Thestor (dragged from his chariot like a fish on a line), Erylaus, and nine more in a list. Sarpedon, the Lycian leader, shames his men for running and leaps down to face the man who has loosed so many knees; Patroclus leaps down to meet him, and they close like two screaming vultures. Zeus pities them and asks Hera whether to snatch his son Sarpedon out of the battle alive or let Patroclus kill him. Hera answers sharply: will he really free from death a mortal long fated? Let him, but the other gods will not all approve, and each may then want to save his own son; she tells him to let Sarpedon die and then send Death and Sleep to carry the body home to Lycia for burial. Zeus obeys and pours bloody drops on the ground for his son. In the fight Patroclus kills Sarpedon’s attendant Thrasymelus; Sarpedon misses Patroclus but wounds the trace-horse Pedasus, who falls dying and tangles the team, until Automedon cuts him free and the two men close again.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν πρώτας ἐπέκερσε φάλαγγας,
ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ἔεργε παλιμπετές,
sentences.l:
And Patroclus, when then the first battle-lines he had cut off,
back to the ships kept them hemmed, backward,
sentences.i: Now when Patroclus had cut off the foremost battle-lines, he kept them hemmed back toward the ships, driving them backward,
sentences.n: A new part begins at a paragraph break; the subject is Patroclus, who is cutting the fleeing Trojans off from their city and driving them back toward the ships. ἐπέκερσε is the aorist of ἐπικείρω ‘cut off, shear’, said of battle-lines (φάλαγγας), and ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘when then’. ἔεργε is the imperfect of ἔργω ‘shut in, keep’, so ‘kept them hemmed’, with ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ‘back toward the ships’. παλιμπετές is an adverb ‘backward’; its formation (πάλιν plus a root meaning ‘fall’ or ‘fly’) is not certain.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ πόληος
εἴα ἱεμένους ἐπιβαινέμεν,
sentences.l:
and of the city did not
allow them, eager, to set foot on it,
sentences.i: and would not let them, eager as they were, set foot in the city,
sentences.n: οὐδὲ … εἴα is ‘and did not allow’, the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’. ἱεμένους is the masculine plural participle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, the object of εἴα. ἐπιβαινέμεν is the infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step on, set foot on’ in the Aeolic form with -μεν, and it takes the genitive πόληος, ‘of the city’ (πόλις ‘city’, the Trojans’ own town, to which they were running). The Trojans are not named in the unit; they are the object throughout.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μεσηγὺ
νηῶν καὶ ποταμοῦ καὶ τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο
κτεῖνε μεταΐσσων,
sentences.l:
but in the middle between
the ships and the river and the high wall
he kept killing, darting among them,
sentences.i: but, darting among them, he killed them in the space between the ships, the river and the high wall,
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets what he did against what he stopped. μεσηγύ is ‘in the middle between’ and takes the genitives that follow, νηῶν ‘of the ships’, ποταμοῦ ‘of the river’ (the Scamander) and τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο ‘of the high wall’ (Troy’s wall). κτεῖνε is the imperfect of κτείνω ‘kill’, ‘kept killing’. μεταΐσσων is the participle of μεταΐσσω ‘dart after, dart among’.

sentences.t: πολέων δ’ ἀπετίνυτο ποινήν.
sentences.l: and for many he exacted requital.
sentences.i: and he took requital for many.
sentences.n: ἀπετίνυτο is the imperfect middle of ἀποτίνυμαι ‘exact payment’, and ποινή is ‘requital’, a payment demanded for a killing. πολέων is the genitive plural ‘of many’, and the Greek leaves open who the many are; the natural reading is the Achaeans killed at the ships, whom he now avenges. The word is not the same as ἄποινα ‘ransom’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἤτοι Πρόνοον πρῶτον βάλε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
στέρνον γυμνωθέντα παρ’ ἀσπίδα, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα·
sentences.l:
There indeed Pronous first he struck with his shining spear
in the chest, laid bare beside the shield, and loosed his limbs;
sentences.i: Then he struck Pronous first, with his shining spear, in the chest, which was bared beside his shield, and loosed his limbs;
sentences.n: A run of single kills begins; the names in them are victims, and each is the object of a verb. ἔνθ’ ἤτοι is ‘there indeed’. Πρόνοον ‘Pronous’ is an accusative, and πρῶτον ‘first’ is an adverb. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with his shining spear’, the stock phrase. στέρνον γυμνωθέντα is ‘the chest, laid bare’, an accusative of the part struck, with the aorist passive participle of γυμνόω. λῦσε δὲ γυῖα ‘and loosed his limbs’ is the idiom for killing; the second line is the same line as 16.312, where Menelaus kills Thoas.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών·
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.n: δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘thud, make a dull sound’, and πεσών the aorist participle ‘having fallen’, so the Greek says ‘thudded, having fallen’ and the English joins the two as ‘fell with a thud’. The subject is Pronous.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ Θέστορα Ἤνοπος υἱὸν
δεύτερον ὁρμηθείς·
sentences.l:
and Thestor, Enops’ son,
second he rushed at;
sentences.i: Then he rushed at Thestor, son of Enops, next;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is Patroclus again. Θέστορα is the accusative of the victim, Ἤνοπος υἱόν ‘son of Enops’, and δεύτερον ‘second’ is an adverb, ‘next, as the second’. ὁρμηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, here with an accusative of the man rushed at; the sentence has no finite verb of its own and its main verb νύξε comes in 404 after the picture of Thestor. Ἤνοπος is a man’s name here, not the adjective ἤνοπι of 408.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν εὐξέστῳ ἐνὶ δίφρῳ
ἧστο ἀλείς·
sentences.l:
he, on the one hand, in his well-polished chariot
sat crouched;
sentences.i: He was sitting crouched in his well-polished chariot;
sentences.n: ὃ μέν is Thestor, set against ὃ δέ ‘and he’ (Patroclus) in 404. εὐξέστῳ ἐνὶ δίφρῳ is ‘in his well-polished chariot’ (ἐΰξεστος ‘well-polished’, δίφρος ‘chariot’, ἐνί the poetic ‘in’). ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ἀλείς is a passive participle, probably ‘crouched, huddled up’ and related to εἰλέω ‘press together’; the form is rare and the sense is taken from the line.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γὰρ πλήγη φρένας, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρῶν
ἡνία ἠΐχθησαν·
sentences.l:
for he was struck out of his mind, and out of his hands
the reins darted;
sentences.i: for he was struck out of his mind, and the reins darted out of his hands;
sentences.n: ἐκ … πλήγη is ‘was struck out’, the aorist passive of ἐκπλήσσω, with φρένας as an accusative of respect, ‘in his mind’, so the whole is ‘struck out of his mind’ with terror. In the second half ἐκ … χειρῶν is ‘out of his hands’, and ἡνία ‘reins’ is a neuter plural with the plural verb ἠΐχθησαν, the aorist passive of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, the verb used of a spear leaving the palm at 3.367–368. δ’ ἄρα here only continues.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἔγχεϊ νύξε παραστὰς
γναθμὸν δεξιτερόν, διὰ δ’ αὐτοῦ πεῖρεν ὀδόντων,
sentences.l:
and he with his spear stabbed him, standing beside him,
in the right jaw, and through his teeth drove it,
sentences.i: and Patroclus stood beside him, stabbed him with his spear in the right jaw, and drove it through his teeth,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Patroclus. νύξε is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’, παραστάς the aorist participle ‘standing beside’, and γναθμὸν δεξιτερόν ‘the right jaw’ the part struck. διὰ … πεῖρεν is a split verb, διαπείρω ‘drive through’, and the object ‘it’ (the spear) is not spoken. αὐτοῦ ‘his’ goes with ὀδόντων and stands apart from it, so the clause is ‘through his teeth’.

sentences.t: ἕλκε δὲ δουρὸς ἑλὼν ὑπὲρ ἄντυγος,
sentences.l: and he dragged him, having taken hold by the spear, over the rail,
sentences.i: and, taking hold of the spear, dragged him with it over the chariot’s rail,
sentences.n: ἕλκε is the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘drag’, and ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’; with the genitive δουρός it means ‘taking hold by the spear’, so the spear is the handle. ἄντυγος is the genitive of ἄντυξ, the rail of a chariot-body, and ὑπέρ makes it ‘over the rail’. The man dragged is Thestor, not spoken.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὅτε τις φὼς
πέτρῃ ἔπι προβλῆτι καθήμενος ἱερὸν ἰχθὺν
ἐκ πόντοιο θύραζε λίνῳ καὶ ἤνοπι χαλκῷ·
sentences.i: just as a man sitting on a jutting rock drags a sacred fish out of the sea onto the land with line and gleaming bronze;
sentences.n: A simile begins, and the verb ‘drags’ (ἕλκε of 406) is carried over from the first half of this same line; ὣς in 409 answers it. φώς is ‘man’. πέτρῃ … προβλῆτι is ‘a jutting rock’ (προβλής ‘thrust forward’). ἱερὸν ἰχθύν is ‘a sacred fish’: ἱερός is ‘sacred’ and why a fish is called so is not known. θύραζε is ‘to the outside’, out onto the land. λίνῳ is ‘with a line’. ἤνοπι is an adjective of bronze, traditionally ‘gleaming’; its sense is not certain. The bronze is the hook.

sentences.t: ὣς ἕλκ’ ἐκ δίφροιο κεχηνότα δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
sentences.l: so he dragged him from the chariot, gaping, with the shining spear,
sentences.i: so he dragged him gaping out of the chariot with his shining spear,
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile. ἕλκ’ is ἕλκε ‘dragged’, and ἐκ δίφροιο ‘out of the chariot’. κεχηνότα is the perfect participle of χαίνω ‘gape’, accusative to agree with the unspoken ‘him’, so Thestor’s mouth hangs open as the fish’s does. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is again ‘with the shining spear’; the spear is the hook of the simile.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ στόμ’ ἔωσε·
sentences.l: and down on his mouth he thrust him;
sentences.i: and thrust him down on his face;
sentences.n: κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ … ἔωσε is a split verb: κάδ is κατά with its last letter changed before δ, and with ἔωσε, the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, it makes ‘thrust down’. ἐπὶ στόμα is ‘on his mouth’, which is to say face down. The word for the object, ‘him’, is not spoken.

sentences.t: πεσόντα δέ μιν λίπε θυμός.
sentences.l: and as he fell, his life left him.
sentences.i: and as he fell, his life left him.
sentences.n: πεσόντα is the aorist participle ‘having fallen’, accusative to agree with μιν ‘him’, which comes after it; λίπε is the aorist of λείπω ‘leave’. θυμός is ‘life’ here, what leaves a man in death. This is Thestor’s death.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ Ἐρύλαον ἐπεσσύμενον βάλε πέτρῳ
μέσσην κὰκ κεφαλήν·
sentences.l:
And next Erylaus, as he rushed at him, he struck with a stone
down on the middle of the head;
sentences.i: Next, as Erylaus rushed upon him, he struck him with a stone in the middle of the head;
sentences.n: A third victim. Ἐρύλαον is an accusative, and ἐπεσσύμενον is the perfect participle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’, with present force, ‘as he rushed on’. βάλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’, and πέτρῳ is the dative ‘with a stone’; this πέτρος is a stone, not the rock (πέτρη) of the simile. μέσσην κὰκ κεφαλήν is ‘in the middle of the head’, with κὰκ the form of κατά before κ.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄνδιχα πᾶσα κεάσθη
ἐν κόρυθι βριαρῇ·
sentences.l:
and it was split in two, the whole of it,
inside the weighty helmet;
sentences.i: and the whole head was split in two inside the heavy helmet;
sentences.n: ἣ is feminine and takes up κεφαλήν ‘head’. ἄνδιχα is ‘in two’, πᾶσα ‘the whole of it’, and κεάσθη is the aorist passive of κεάζω ‘split’. The head was split inside the helmet, which the next unit says. ἐν κόρυθι βριαρῇ is ‘in the heavy helmet’, κόρυς ‘helmet’ (dative) and βριαρός ‘weighty, heavy’. The helmet is the one Erylaus wears. The verb for the splitting is in the line before.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα πρηνὴς ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κάππεσεν, ἀμφὶ δέ μιν θάνατος χύτο θυμοραϊστής.
sentences.l:
and he, face down, onto the earth
fell down, and about him death was poured, life-destroying.
sentences.i: and he fell face down upon the earth, and death, the destroyer of life, was poured about him.
sentences.n: πρηνής is ‘face down’. κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν, the aorist of καταπίπτω ‘fall down’. ἀμφὶ δέ μιν … χύτο is ‘about him was poured’, χύτο the aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’ with a passive sense. θάνατος θυμοραϊστής is ‘death, the destroyer of life’: θυμός is ‘life’ and the second part is from a verb meaning ‘shatter’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ Ἐρύμαντα καὶ Ἀμφοτερὸν καὶ Ἐπάλτην
Τληπόλεμόν τε Δαμαστορίδην Ἐχίον τε Πύριν τε
Ἰφέα τ’ Εὔιππόν τε καὶ Ἀργεάδην Πολύμηλον
πάντας ἐπασσυτέρους πέλασε χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ.
sentences.l:
And next Erymas and Amphoterus and Epaltes
and Tlepolemus, Damastor’s-son, and Echius and Pyris
and Ipheus and Euippus and Polymelus, Argeas’-son,
all one close upon another he brought to the much-nourishing earth.
sentences.i: Next he brought down Erymas, and Amphoterus, and Epaltes, Tlepolemus son of Damastor, Echius and Pyris, Ipheus and Euippus, and Polymelus son of Argeas, bringing them all down one after another to the earth that feeds so many.
sentences.n: Nine names at once, all accusatives, all victims; the verb, πέλασε ‘brought near’ (here ‘brought down’), comes only in 418, and πάντας ‘all of them’ gathers the list. The Greek tells us nothing about these men beyond their names. Δαμαστορίδην ‘son of Damastor’ and Ἀργεάδην ‘son of Argeas’ are patronymics. This Erymas is not the Erymas killed at 16.345, and this Tlepolemus is not the Rhodian. ἐπασσυτέρους is ‘one close upon another’; πουλυβοτείρῃ is ‘much-nourishing’, an epithet of the earth.

sentences.t:
Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἴδ’ ἀμιτροχίτωνας ἑταίρους
χέρσ’ ὕπο Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο δαμέντας,
sentences.l:
And Sarpedon, when then he saw his companions in tunic and girdle
subdued under the hands of Patroclus, Menoetius’-son,
sentences.i: Now when Sarpedon saw his companions, clad in tunic and girdle, subdued under the hands of Patroclus, son of Menoetius,
sentences.n: Σαρπηδών is the Lycian leader. ἀμιτροχίτωνας is built from μίτρη, the belt-guard worn under the corselet, and χιτών ‘tunic’; the usual explanation is that the men wear both, but the first letter ἀ- is not understood and the word’s sense is not certain. ἑταίρους is ‘companions’. χέρσ’ ὕπο Πατρόκλοιο is ‘under the hands of Patroclus’ (χέρσ’ for χερσί), and δαμέντας is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, meaning killed. Μενοιτιάδαο is the patronymic ‘son of Menoetius’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: κέκλετ’ ἄρ’ ἀντιθέοισι καθαπτόμενος Λυκίοισιν·
sentences.l: he gave orders to the godlike Lycians, accosting them:
sentences.i: he gave orders to the godlike Lycians, addressing them directly:
sentences.n: κέκλετο is the aorist of κέλομαι, and the house rendering is ‘gave orders to’ although what follows is a rebuke. ἀντιθέοισι Λυκίοισιν is ‘to the godlike Lycians’, ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ and the dative plural. καθαπτόμενος is the participle of καθάπτομαι ‘lay hold of, address directly’, the speech introduction that comes before a hard word.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς ὦ Λύκιοι·
sentences.l: “Shame, O Lycians!
sentences.i: “Shame, Lycians!
sentences.n: αἰδώς is a nominative, ‘shame’, used as a cry, as in the cry ‘Shame, Argives’ at 5.787. ὦ Λύκιοι is ‘O Lycians’, the vocative. Sarpedon’s speech begins, and it runs to line 425.

sentences.t: πόσε φεύγετε; νῦν θοοὶ ἔστε.
sentences.l: Whither do you flee? Now be swift.
sentences.i: Where are you fleeing to? Now be quick.
sentences.n: πόσε is ‘to where’, and φεύγετε the present ‘you are fleeing’; the clause is a question, marked with the Greek question mark. θοοί is ‘swift’ and ἔστε the imperative of εἰμί ‘be’: ‘now be swift’ is a call for quickness, and the Greek does not say for what; the next lines show it is for turning to face the enemy. The question about fleeing is set against the quickness he asks for.

sentences.t:
ἀντήσω γὰρ ἐγὼ τοῦδ’ ἀνέρος, ὄφρα δαείω
ὅς τις ὅδε κρατέει καὶ δὴ κακὰ πολλὰ ἔοργε
Τρῶας, ἐπεὶ πολλῶν τε καὶ ἐσθλῶν γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν.
sentences.l:
For I will meet this man myself, so that I may learn
whoever this is who prevails, and has already done many evils
to the Trojans, since the knees of many and good men he has loosed.”
sentences.i: For I myself will meet this man, so that I may learn whoever he is who is prevailing and has already done the Trojans many evils, since he has loosed the knees of many good men.”
sentences.n: ἀντήσω is the future of ἀντάω ‘meet’, which takes the genitive τοῦδ’ ἀνέρος ‘this man’ (Patroclus is not named); ἐγώ makes the ‘I’ strong. ὄφρα δαείω is ‘so that I may learn’, δαείω the aorist subjunctive of δάω ‘learn’. ὅς τις ὅδε is ‘whoever this man is’, the indirect question after it. κρατέει is ‘prevails’, and καὶ δή … ἔοργε ‘has already done’, ἔοργε the perfect of ῥέζω ‘do’. γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν ‘loosed the knees’ is the idiom for killing, and the speech ends on it. Both lines also stand at 5.175–176.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε.
sentences.l: He spoke, and from the chariot with his armour leapt to the ground;
sentences.i: So he said, and leapt from the chariot to the ground with his armour;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα is ‘he spoke’, ἦ being the imperfect of ἠμί ‘say’ and ῥα the particle ἄρα, and καί continues to the act. ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’ (a plural, ὄχεα, ‘the chariot’), σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘with his armour’, and ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’. χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’. Sarpedon fights on foot, as Patroclus does. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐπεὶ ἴδεν ἔκθορε δίφρου.
sentences.l: And Patroclus, from the other side, when he saw him, leapt out of his chariot.
sentences.i: And Patroclus, seeing him from the other side, leapt down out of his chariot.
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’, and ἴδεν is εἶδεν, the aorist of ὁράω ‘see’, with Sarpedon as the unspoken object. ἔκθορε is the aorist of ἐκθρῴσκω ‘leap out’, and δίφρου the genitive ‘out of the chariot’. The mirror of 426: each man gets down so as to meet the other on foot.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὥς τ’ αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες ἀγκυλοχεῖλαι
πέτρῃ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῇ μεγάλα κλάζοντε μάχωνται,
sentences.l:
And they, like vultures, crook-taloned, hook-beaked,
that on a high rock, screaming loudly, the two fight,
sentences.i: And they were like hook-taloned, hook-beaked vultures that fight on a high rock, the pair of them screaming loudly,
sentences.n: A simile. αἰγυπιοί are ‘vultures’, γαμψώνυχες ‘crook-taloned’ and ἀγκυλοχεῖλαι ‘hook-beaked’, two stock epithets. πέτρῃ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῇ is ‘on a high rock’. κλάζοντε is a dual participle, ‘the two screaming’, and the dual shows that only a pair fights. μάχωνται is a subjunctive, the mood of a general comparison, ‘as vultures fight’. ὥς τ’ ‘like’ links the men to the birds.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ κεκλήγοντες ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ὄρουσαν.
sentences.l: so they, shrieking, leapt at one another.
sentences.i: so they, shrieking, leapt at one another.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile. κεκλήγοντες is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek’ used as a present, ‘shrieking’, and ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ὄρουσαν is ‘leapt at one another’, ὄρουσαν the aorist of ὀρούω ‘leap, rush’. The cry of the birds is carried over to the men.

sentences.t: τοὺς δὲ ἰδὼν ἐλέησε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω,
sentences.l: And them seeing, pitied them the son of Cronus of crooked cunning,
sentences.i: And when the son of Cronus of crooked cunning saw them, he pitied them,
sentences.n: Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω is ‘the son of Cronus of crooked cunning’, Zeus without his name; ἀγκυλομήτεω is a genitive agreeing with Κρόνου, and its first part is ἀγκύλος ‘crooked’ and its second μῆτις ‘cunning’. τοὺς … ἰδών is ‘seeing them’, the two warriors, and ἐλέησε is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’.

sentences.t: Ἥρην δὲ προσέειπε κασιγνήτην ἄλοχόν τε·
sentences.l: and to Hera he spoke, his sister and wife:
sentences.i: and he spoke to Hera, his sister and his wife:
sentences.n: Ἥρην is the accusative with προσέειπε ‘addressed, spoke to’. κασιγνήτην is ‘sister’ and ἄλοχον ‘wife’; both are feminine accusatives in apposition to Hera, and Zeus and Hera are brother and sister in the story. The colon opens Zeus’s speech, which runs to 438.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγών, ὅ τέ μοι Σαρπηδόνα φίλτατον ἀνδρῶν
μοῖρ’ ὑπὸ Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο δαμῆναι.
sentences.l:
“Oh me, I—that Sarpedon, of men dearest to me,
it is fate under Patroclus, Menoetius’-son, to be subdued.
sentences.i: “Oh me, that Sarpedon, the dearest of men to me, is fated to be subdued by Patroclus, son of Menoetius.
sentences.n: ὤ μοι ἐγών is the cry ‘Oh me, I’, with ἐγών the strong ‘I’. ὅ τε is ‘that’, and what follows is the cause of the cry: Σαρπηδόνα is the accusative subject of the infinitive δαμῆναι ‘to be subdued’, and μοῖρα (μοῖρ’) is ‘fate’ with no verb, so ‘fate it is’. φίλτατον ἀνδρῶν is ‘dearest of men’, a superlative with the genitive. ὑπὸ Πατρόκλοιο is ‘by Patroclus’, the agent. ‘Subdued’ means killed.

sentences.t: διχθὰ δέ μοι κραδίη μέμονε φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντι,
sentences.l: In two ways my heart is bent, as I ponder in my mind,
sentences.i: My heart is bent two ways as I ponder it in my mind,
sentences.n: διχθά is ‘in two ways’, an adverb. κραδίη is ‘heart’, and μέμονε is the perfect of an old verb meaning ‘be eager, be bent’ with a present sense. φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντι is ‘as I ponder in my mind’, with ὁρμαίνοντι a dative participle agreeing with the μοι of the same line, ‘for me, pondering’; ὁρμαίνω is ‘ponder’. The two ways come in the next three lines.

sentences.t:
ἤ μιν ζωὸν ἐόντα μάχης ἄπο δακρυοέσσης
θείω ἀναρπάξας Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ,
sentences.l:
whether him, being alive, away from tearful battle
I should set, having snatched him up, in Lycia’s rich land,
sentences.i: whether I should snatch him up alive from the tearful battle and set him down in the rich land of Lycia,
sentences.n: ἤ opens the first way, and its pair is ἦ in 438. ζωὸν ἐόντα is ‘being alive’. μάχης ἄπο δακρυοέσσης is ‘away from tearful battle’ (δακρυόεις ‘tearful’; ἄπο after its noun). θείω is the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι ‘set’, a deliberative mood, ‘should I set’, with ἀναρπάξας ‘having snatched up’. Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ is ‘in the rich land of Lycia’ (δῆμος ‘land’, πίων ‘rich, fat’).

sentences.t: ἦ ἤδη ὑπὸ χερσὶ Μενοιτιάδαο δαμάσσω.
sentences.l: or now under the hands of Menoetius’-son I should subdue him.”
sentences.i: or should I now have him subdued by the hands of Menoetius’ son.”
sentences.n: ἦ is ‘or’, the second way, answering ἤ of 436; the line has no question mark in this text though it is a deliberation. δαμάσσω is the subjunctive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, ‘should I subdue’. ὑπὸ χερσὶ … Μενοιτιάδαο is ‘under the hands of Menoetius’ son’, the phrase of 420 turned round; Patroclus is not named, and the idea is that Zeus would hand him over to Patroclus to be killed.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.l: Him then answered ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is masculine, so Zeus is the one answered. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is Hera’s stock epithet; the usual explanation is large, calm eyes like an ox’s, but the Greek does not say. πότνια is ‘lady’. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: αἰνότατε is the vocative of αἰνότατος, the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, sharp rather than respectful. Κρονίδη is the patronymic vocative, ‘son of Cronus’, and ποῖον τὸν μῦθον is ‘what sort of word (is) this word’, the article giving ‘this’. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’ in its epic form. The text here ends the line with a full stop, though the sense is a question.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρα θνητὸν ἐόντα πάλαι πεπρωμένον αἴσῃ
ἂψ ἐθέλεις θανάτοιο δυσηχέος ἐξαναλῦσαι;
sentences.l:
A man, being mortal, long since fated by his lot,
back do you wish to loose from ill-sounding death?
sentences.i: Do you wish to loose a man, mortal as he is and long since fated by his lot, back out of ill-sounding death?
sentences.n: ἄνδρα is the object of ἐξαναλῦσαι, ‘to loose out’, an aorist infinitive of ἐξαναλύω built on λύω ‘loose’; ἂψ ‘back’ and the genitive θανάτοιο ‘from death’ complete it. θνητὸν ἐόντα is ‘being mortal’, and πεπρωμένον is a perfect passive participle of πόρω ‘give’ used of what is allotted, ‘fated’, with αἴσῃ ‘by his lot’. δυσηχής is ‘ill-sounding’, δυσ- plus ἦχος ‘sound’.

sentences.t: ἔρδ’· ἀτὰρ οὔ τοι πάντες ἐπαινέομεν θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l: Do it; but we do not all approve, the other gods.
sentences.i: Do it; but we other gods do not all approve.
sentences.n: ἔρδ’ is ἔρδε, the present imperative of ἔρδω ‘do’, here ‘go on, then’, with a stop after it. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, and τοι is a particle of emphasis that the English does not carry. The whole line is one that stands elsewhere in the Iliad, and its English is the same. ἐπαινέομεν is ‘we approve’, with πάντες θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘all the other gods’ for the subject, and οὔ at the start negates πάντες, so ‘not all’.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο is ‘another thing’, τοι ‘to you’, and ἐρέω the future of ἐρέω ‘say, tell’. σὺ δ’ … βάλλεο is the middle imperative of βάλλω ‘put’, with ἐνὶ φρεσὶ σῇσιν ‘in your own mind’ and the object left unsaid, ‘it’; σῇσιν is an old dative plural. The same line recurs elsewhere in the Iliad.

sentences.t: αἴ κε ζὼν πέμψῃς Σαρπηδόνα ὃν δὲ δόμον δέ,
sentences.l: If you send Sarpedon, living, to his own house,
sentences.i: If you send Sarpedon living to his own house,
sentences.n: αἴ κε … πέμψῃς is ‘if you send’, an aorist subjunctive with the particle κε in the future-looking condition. ζών is the participle ‘living’. ὃν δὲ δόμον δέ is ‘to his own house’: ὃν is ‘his own’, δόμον ‘house’, and the ending -δε on the noun adds ‘to’. The first δέ is only a particle and is not translated. The result comes at 446, with φράζεο.

sentences.t:
φράζεο μή τις ἔπειτα θεῶν ἐθέλῃσι καὶ ἄλλος
πέμπειν ὃν φίλον υἱὸν ἀπὸ κρατερῆς ὑσμίνης·
sentences.l:
take heed lest some other god too then wish
to send his own dear son from the strong battle;
sentences.i: take care lest some other god, too, then want to send his own dear son away from the strong battle;
sentences.n: φράζεο is the middle imperative of φράζομαι ‘take heed, consider’, and μή τις … ἐθέλῃσι is ‘lest someone wish’, a subjunctive after the warning. καὶ ἄλλος is ‘and another’, ‘another also’; ‘other’ because Zeus is one such god. πέμπειν is the infinitive ‘to send’ and ὃν φίλον υἱόν ‘his own dear son’. ἀπὸ κρατερῆς ὑσμίνης is ‘from the strong battle’.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ γὰρ περὶ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο μάχονται
υἱέες ἀθανάτων, τοῖσιν κότον αἰνὸν ἐνήσεις.
sentences.l:
for many around the great town of Priam fight,
sons of immortals, in them a fearsome resentment you will put.
sentences.i: for many sons of the immortals are fighting around the great town of Priam, and you will put a fearsome resentment in them.
sentences.n: ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο is ‘the great town of Priam’ (ἄστυ ‘town’, Troy). υἱέες ἀθανάτων is ‘sons of immortals’, meaning heroes who are children of gods, as Sarpedon is; the Greek names none of them. μάχονται is ‘they fight’. τοῖσιν is ‘in them’, κότον αἰνόν ‘a fearsome resentment’ (κότος ‘resentment’), and ἐνήσεις is the future of ἐνίημι ‘put in’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ εἴ τοι φίλος ἐστί, τεὸν δ’ ὀλοφύρεται ἦτορ,
sentences.l: But if he is dear to you, and your heart grieves for him,
sentences.i: But if he is dear to you, and your heart grieves for him,
sentences.n: φίλος ἐστί is ‘is dear’, with τοι ‘to you’. τεόν is the epic form of σόν ‘your’, and ὀλοφύρεται is ‘grieves for’, from ὀλοφύρομαι, with ἦτορ ‘heart’ as its subject. The sentence gives Zeus a condition before the advice that follows.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μέν μιν ἔασον ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ
χέρσ’ ὕπο Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο δαμῆναι·
sentences.l:
indeed, on the one hand, allow him, in the strong battle,
under the hands of Patroclus, Menoetius’-son, to be subdued;
sentences.i: indeed, allow him, in the strong battle, to be subdued under the hands of Patroclus, son of Menoetius;
sentences.n: ἤτοι μέν is ‘indeed, on the one hand’, answered by αὐτάρ in 453. ἔασον is the aorist imperative of ἐάω ‘allow’, with μιν ‘him’ and the infinitive δαμῆναι ‘to be subdued’ (aorist passive of δάμνημι). The first half of the advice is the reverse of what Hera describes in 441–442: let the death come.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ τόν γε λίπῃ ψυχή τε καὶ αἰών,
sentences.l: but when his soul and life have left him,
sentences.i: but when his soul and his life have left him,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is ‘but when’ (ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν). λίπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of λείπω ‘leave’, here a singular verb with two subjects. ψυχή is ‘soul’ and αἰών ‘life’; the two are named together as what leaves a dying man. τόν γε ‘him, that one’ is Sarpedon.

sentences.t:
πέμπειν μιν θάνατόν τε φέρειν καὶ νήδυμον ὕπνον
εἰς ὅ κε δὴ Λυκίης εὐρείης δῆμον ἵκωνται,
sentences.l:
send him, Death and sweet Sleep to carry him,
until they come to the land of wide Lycia,
sentences.i: send him off, with Death and sweet Sleep to carry him, until they reach the land of wide Lycia,
sentences.n: πέμπειν is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘send’, with μιν ‘him’ as the object. θάνατον and ὕπνον are accusatives that serve as the subjects of the infinitive φέρειν ‘to carry’, and the Greek has no word for ‘with’ or ‘let’. Θάνατος and Ὕπνος are two gods, here named as persons. νήδυμος is traditionally ‘sweet’, but where the word comes from is not known. εἰς ὅ κε is ‘until’, with ἵκωνται the subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come, reach’; the subject is ‘they’, Death and Sleep with the body. Λυκίης εὐρείης is ‘wide Lycia’ and δῆμον ‘land’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά ἑ ταρχύσουσι κασίγνητοί τε ἔται τε
τύμβῳ τε στήλῃ τε·
sentences.l:
there his brothers and kinsmen will bury him
with a tomb and a pillar;
sentences.i: there his brothers and kinsmen will bury him with a tomb and a pillar;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’ and ἑ ‘him’. ταρχύσουσι is the future of ταρχύω ‘bury’, a funeral word of unknown origin. κασίγνητοι are ‘brothers’ and ἔται ‘kinsmen’ (nominative plural of ἔτης). τύμβῳ ‘with a tomb’ and στήλῃ ‘with a pillar’ are datives of means; the pillar is the upright stone set on the tomb.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων.
sentences.l: for that is the prize of the dead.”
sentences.i: for that is the prize of honour that belongs to the dead.”
sentences.n: τό is ‘that’, the burial just named. γέρας is ‘prize’, or in the free English ‘prize of honour’, the share due to a person, and θανόντων is the aorist participle of θνῄσκω in the genitive plural, ‘of those who have died’. This sentence is the reason for the advice, and with it Hera’s speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and did not disobey, the father of men and of gods;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the father of men and of gods did not disobey her;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο is ‘so she spoke’, closing the speech. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε is ‘the father of men and of gods’, Zeus, and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
αἱματοέσσας δὲ ψιάδας κατέχευεν ἔραζε
παῖδα φίλον τιμῶν, τόν οἱ Πάτροκλος ἔμελλε
φθίσειν ἐν Τροίῃ ἐριβώλακι τηλόθι πάτρης.
sentences.l:
and bloody drops he poured down upon the ground,
honouring his dear son, whom Patroclus was destined
to destroy in rich-soiled Troy, far from his fatherland.
sentences.i: and he poured bloody drops down upon the ground, honouring his dear son, whom Patroclus was to kill in Troy of the rich soil, far from his native land.
sentences.n: αἱματοέσσας is ‘bloody’ (accusative plural of αἱματόεις), and ψιάδας is the rare word ‘drops’, taken from the context and the old gloss; its origin is not known. κατέχευεν is the aorist of καταχέω ‘pour down’, ἔραζε ‘to the ground’. τιμῶν is ‘honouring’, παῖδα φίλον ‘dear son’; τόν is the relative and οἱ ‘for him’, Zeus. μέλλω with an infinitive is ‘be destined to’, φθίσειν a future infinitive of φθίω ‘destroy’. ἐριβώλακι is ‘rich-soiled’, and τηλόθι πάτρης ‘far from his fatherland’, Lycia.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
sentences.l: And when they were near, going against one another,
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, Patroclus and Sarpedon. ὅτε δή is ‘when’ and σχεδόν ‘near’. ἦσαν is the imperfect of εἰμί ‘were’, ἰόντες the participle of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ‘at one another’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἤτοι Πάτροκλος ἀγακλειτὸν Θρασύμηλον,
ὅς ῥ’ ἠῢς θεράπων Σαρπηδόνος ἦεν ἄνακτος,
τὸν βάλε νείαιραν κατὰ γαστέρα, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l:
There indeed Patroclus renowned Thrasymelus,
who was the good attendant of lord Sarpedon,
him he struck in the lower belly, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.i: Then Patroclus struck the renowned Thrasymelus, who was the good attendant of lord Sarpedon, in the lower belly, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.n: Θρασύμηλον is the object, and its relative clause fills line 464: ἀγακλειτός is ‘renowned’, ἠῢς θεράπων ‘good attendant’ and ἄναξ ‘lord’ (ἄνακτος, the genitive). ῥ’ in ὅς ῥ’ is the particle ἄρα. τὸν βάλε in 465 takes the man up again, ‘him he struck’. νείαιραν is an adjective on γαστέρα ‘belly’, ‘lower’ (from νέατος ‘lowest’), and the form is rare. λῦσε δὲ γυῖα is the idiom ‘loosed his limbs’, killed.

sentences.t:
Σαρπηδὼν δ’ αὐτοῦ μὲν ἀπήμβροτε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
δεύτερον ὁρμηθείς,
sentences.l:
And Sarpedon missed him with his shining spear,
rushing second,
sentences.i: And Sarpedon, rushing second, missed him with his shining spear,
sentences.n: ἀπήμβροτε is the aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’, and αὐτοῦ is the genitive ‘him’ (Patroclus), the case that verb takes. δεύτερον ὁρμηθείς is ‘rushing second’, the same phrase as at 402 and now of Sarpedon; his throw is the second of the fight. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is again ‘with the shining spear’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ Πήδασον οὔτασεν ἵππον
ἔγχεϊ δεξιὸν ὦμον·
sentences.l:
but he wounded the horse Pedasus
with his spear in the right shoulder;
sentences.i: but he wounded the horse Pedasus in the right shoulder with his spear;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is Sarpedon, set against αὐτοῦ, Patroclus, whom he missed in the line before. Πήδασον … ἵππον is ‘the horse Pedasus’, the third horse in Achilles’ team, the mortal one, harnessed at the side of the immortal pair (see 16.152). οὔτασεν is the aorist of οὐτάζω ‘wound’, ἔγχεϊ ‘with his spear’, and δεξιὸν ὦμον ‘the right shoulder’ is an accusative of the part struck.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔβραχε θυμὸν ἀΐσθων,
sentences.l: and he bellowed, gasping out his life,
sentences.i: and he bellowed as he gasped out his life,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is the horse. ἔβραχε is the aorist of βράχω, a verb for a loud sound; it is the word used of Ares’ cry at 5.859, and ‘bellowed’ is kept. θυμὸν ἀΐσθων is ‘gasping out his life’: θυμός is ‘life’, and ἀΐσθω is a rare verb for breathing out, gasping, whose origin is not known.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μακών, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔπτατο θυμός.
sentences.l: and down he fell in the dust, crying out, and away flew his life.
sentences.i: he fell down in the dust with a cry, and his life flew away.
sentences.n: κάδ is κατά before δ, joined in a split verb with ἔπεσ’ (ἔπεσε), ‘fell down’. ἐν κονίῃσι is ‘in the dust’ and μακών the aorist participle of μηκάομαι ‘cry out’, the cry of an animal. ἀπὸ … ἔπτατο is ‘flew away’, from πέτομαι, the soul taking off like a bird. θυμός here is ‘life’. The same line stands in the Odyssey, at the end of a killing there too.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ διαστήτην, κρίκε δὲ ζυγόν,
sentences.l: and the two stood apart, and the yoke creaked,
sentences.i: and the pair stood apart, and the yoke creaked,
sentences.n: τὼ is a dual, ‘the two’, here the two horses of the yoke, the immortal pair Xanthus and Balius. διαστήτην is the dual aorist of διΐστημι ‘stand apart’. κρίκε is the aorist of κρίζω ‘creak’, a rare word, and ζυγόν is ‘yoke’, the beam across their necks. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἡνία δέ σφι
σύγχυτ’, ἐπεὶ δὴ κεῖτο παρήορος ἐν κονίῃσι.
sentences.l:
and their reins
were tangled, since the trace-horse lay in the dust.
sentences.i: and their reins were tangled, since the trace-horse lay in the dust.
sentences.n: ἡνία … σφι is ‘the reins for them’ (σφι ‘for them’). σύγχυτ’ is σύγχυτο, the aorist middle of συγχέω, passive in sense ‘pour together, confuse’, so the reins ran into one another. κεῖτο is ‘lay’ and ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’. παρήορος is ‘the trace-horse’, the horse harnessed alongside the yoked pair by side-straps (παρηορίαι, ‘traces’, at 8.87), here Pedasus. At 7.156 the sense of the same word was not known and ‘stretched out’ was a guess from the line; here the harness meaning is clear and is used.

sentences.t: τοῖο μὲν Αὐτομέδων δουρικλυτὸς εὕρετο τέκμωρ·
sentences.l: Of this Automedon, famed-for-the-spear, found an end;
sentences.i: Automedon, famed for his spear, found a way out of this;
sentences.n: τοῖο is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘of this’, the trouble. Αὐτομέδων is Achilles’ charioteer, now driving Patroclus. δουρικλυτός is ‘famed for his spear’. εὕρετο is the aorist middle of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, and τέκμωρ is ‘an end’ in the literal English and ‘a way out’ in the free English, as in the Odyssey, here the end of the trouble; at 1.526 the same word is ‘a sign’.

sentences.t:
σπασσάμενος τανύηκες ἄορ παχέος παρὰ μηροῦ
ἀΐξας ἀπέκοψε παρήορον οὐδ’ ἐμάτησε·
sentences.l:
drawing the long-pointed sword from beside his stout thigh,
darting, he cut away the trace-horse, and did not hang back;
sentences.i: He drew the long-pointed sword from beside his stout thigh, darted forward, cut the trace-horse away, and did not hang back;
sentences.n: σπασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of σπάω ‘draw’, and τανύηκες is ‘long-pointed’ (the epithet of the sword), with ἄορ ‘sword’. παχέος παρὰ μηροῦ is ‘from beside the stout thigh’; the line is the Odyssey’s, said there of Odysseus with ‘my’. ἀΐξας is ‘darting’ and ἀπέκοψε the aorist of ἀποκόπτω ‘cut off’, here cut loose from the harness. οὐδ’ ἐμάτησε is ‘and did not hang back’, ματάω a rare verb ‘linger’.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἰθυνθήτην, ἐν δὲ ῥυτῆρσι τάνυσθεν·
sentences.l: and the two were set straight, and in the straps were stretched;
sentences.i: and the pair were set straight and pulled taut in the straps;
sentences.n: τώ here is the two horses again, and ἰθυνθήτην is the dual aorist passive of ἰθύνω ‘make straight’. τάνυσθεν is the third-person plural aorist passive of τανύω ‘stretch’, with the pair as its subject. ῥυτῆρσι is the dative plural of ῥυτήρ, a word from ἐρύω ‘draw’, probably the straps they pull by; whether it means traces or reins is not certain, and reins have their own word, ἡνία.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ αὖτις συνίτην ἔριδος πέρι θυμοβόροιο.
sentences.l: and the two again came together over heart-devouring strife.
sentences.i: and the two men came together again in heart-devouring strife.
sentences.n: τώ is a dual again, but this time the two men, Patroclus and Sarpedon, not the horses. συνίτην is the dual imperfect of σύνειμι (εἶμι) ‘come together’, and αὖτις is ‘again’. ἔριδος πέρι is ‘over strife’, ἔρις ‘strife’. θυμοβόρος is ‘heart-devouring’, from θυμός ‘heart’ and the root of βορά ‘food’, ‘eating the heart’. The part ends with the fight begun.
